analysis.one_liner: Bars pharmacy middlemen from pocketing secret drug-price markups and forces them to pass all manufacturer rebates to health plans.
analysis.headline: The Senate health committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in June 2023, but it never received a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs, are the middlemen that negotiate drug prices and pharmacy reimbursements for employer health plans. This bill would require PBMs to give employers detailed reports on what drugs cost, what rebates they receive, and how often prescriptions are steered to pharmacies the PBM owns. It would also ban "spread pricing" — charging a plan more for a drug than the pharmacy was paid — and require PBMs to hand over 100% of manufacturer rebates to the health plan, with civil penalties of up to $10,000 per day for violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families with employer-sponsored health coverage, and the employers who pay for those plans. Full rebate pass-through and the spread-pricing ban would route money that currently stays with PBMs back to health plans, which should show up in premiums, deductibles, and copays. Independent pharmacies also gain from rules that expose PBMs' payment practices.

how_it_helps.text: Bans spread pricing starting in 2025, so PBMs cannot charge a health plan or its members more for a prescription drug than the pharmacy was paid for it, except for narrow pharmacy penalties [S2][S3].

Requires PBMs and pharmacy benefit administrators to remit 100% of manufacturer rebates, fees, and discounts to the health plan within 90 days, and lets plan sponsors audit rebate contracts at least once a year [S3].

Requires annual reports to employers detailing gross and net drug spending, out-of-pocket costs, rebates received, payments to brokers who steered the plan to the PBM, and the rationale for which drugs get preferred placement on the plan's formulary [S3].

Requires six-month reports on prescriptions dispensed by pharmacies the PBM owns, including how the prices charged compare with other network pharmacies, exposing self-dealing inside PBM corporate families [S3].

Bars employers from discriminating against employees because of information in the reports, and sets civil penalties of $10,000 per day for failure to report or comply, plus penalties for knowingly false information [S3].

analysis.who_pays: PBMs — including the largest ones owned by CVS, Cigna, and UnitedHealth — would lose spread-pricing revenue and rebate retention. Drug manufacturers would face disclosure of copay-assistance funding and auditable rebate contracts. Some compliance costs would likely flow to health plans through administrative fees.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not cap drug prices itself; it works through transparency and rebate pass-through, so savings depend on employers actually renegotiating contracts with the newly visible information [S3].

The heaviest reporting duties apply to large-employer plans (50 or more employees); small-employer plans get a narrower report, and coverage offered through insurers is opt-in, so many workers' plans would see limited new transparency [S3].

Violations carry civil penalties of $10,000 per day plus penalties for false information, and PBMs could pass the cost of detailed annual and six-month reporting on to health plans through higher administrative fees [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit — rebates and spread revenue flowing back to health plans instead of staying with PBMs — is substantial for the roughly half of Americans with employer coverage, and the compliance cost of reporting is modest compared with the dollars involved. The main honest caveats are that the bill does not cap drug prices directly, that smaller plans get only partial protections, and that enforcement depends on federal agencies actually pursuing penalties.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in June 2023, but Senate leaders never brought it to the floor for a vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill in April 2023 with a Republican co-lead, Senator Bill Cassidy, plus cosponsors Senator Patty Murray (D), Senator Roger Marshall (R), and Senator Mike Braun (R) [S3][S4].
The Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in May 2023 and formally reported it on June 22, 2023 [S5].
The same day, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 113), which makes it available for floor consideration but does not guarantee a vote [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never reached the Senate floor and expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PBMs and drug manufacturers are better off because the bill died: spread pricing, rebate retention, and current disclosure practices continue unchanged, and employers and insured workers keep bearing the cost. Committee action and bipartisan sponsorship were not enough to get floor time.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator (I-VT), Chairman, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, guided it through committee markup, and reported it to the Senate calendar as committee chair.

for.name: Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Co-led introduction of the bill with Senator Sanders, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.role: Majority and Minority leaders of the 118th Senate
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote despite it sitting on the legislative calendar for more than 18 months; floor time was spent on other business.

against.name: PBM industry (Pharmacy Care Management Association)
against.role: Trade association for the largest pharmacy benefit managers
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against legislation restricting PBM spread pricing and rebate practices during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was an independent and its four cosponsors split 3 Republicans and 1 Democrat, but the chamber's leaders — who decide what gets floor time — never brought it up in either party's agenda.

industries.note: The bill bans spread pricing and forces PBMs to pass 100% of manufacturer rebates to health plans, eliminating their two main sources of hidden revenue. It also exposes how often prescriptions are steered to PBMs' own pharmacies.
The rebate system itself continues, but manufacturers' copay-assistance funding and rebate contracts become visible to employers and auditable, reducing room for opaque pricing arrangements.
Banning spread pricing removes the practice of PBMs paying pharmacies less than they charge plans, and the reporting on PBM-owned pharmacies makes the competitive field more even.
They must disclose broker payments and pass rebates through, but they also gain negotiating leverage over PBMs and clearer information for plan design.
